content: To strengthen health systems holistically, it is essential to address the root causes of systemic issues that contribute to challenges in data quality. Countries should develop or update their strategies to improve both the quality and utilization of data. This includes linking data quality assessments with corrective actions, such as training, supportive supervision, and mentoring. Errors identified in data should be corrected at the point of service delivery within the HIV patient monitoring system. The design of patient monitoring tools should be optimized to enhance data quality and reduce the time healthcare professionals and administrative staff spend on reporting tasks. Periodic reviews of these tools are necessary to ensure alignment with current guidelines, indicator definitions, and patient and data flow processes. Developing job aids, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and site-level orientation for data clerks and healthcare workers involved in recording and entering patient monitoring data can standardize data entry and reporting while improving data quality. Regular monitoring of data completeness is critical. This includes labeling patient records with prompts for healthcare workers to follow up and address incomplete data during subsequent clinic visits. Incomplete data remains a significant challenge, affecting patient care, program indicator accuracy, and resource allocation. Routine data checks, applicable to any data element, can ensure data quality. For example, viral load (VL) data checks should be routinely conducted to improve data quality, strengthen the interface between laboratories and clinics, and support both patient and program management. To conduct VL data checks, the laboratory’s central database or laboratory information systems should be queried by site for the number of samples processed, rejected, and pending. These figures should be compared with site-reported data for VL results received and documented in the VL sample collection logbook or tracking log. Similarly, a line list of high VL clients can be generated from the central database for a specific time period (e.g., monthly) and cross-checked with facility-level records, such as the high VL register and electronic medical record (EMR)-generated data. In facilities without EMRs, patient files may be randomly selected to verify the availability and proper documentation of results, such as the accurate date of VL sample collection and results. High VL results from the central database should also be compared against the facility’s high VL registers for the same period. The site’s high VL cascade should be reviewed to assess the timeliness of receiving VL results and subsequent actions, such as enhanced adherence counseling, repeat VL measurements, multidisciplinary reviews for virologic failures, potential antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimen changes, and follow-up VL testing after regimen switches. Point-of-care (POC) testing for VL has been deployed in many countries to prioritize subpopulations, such as children, adolescents, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and patients with prior high VL, to improve access to VL testing and reduce turnaround times for results. However, the scale-up of POC testing platforms has introduced challenges for data availability, as these platforms do not always integrate with conventional laboratory-based information systems. Data quality checks are critical to ensure the transfer, availability, and completeness of VL data from various settings for effective program monitoring. Frequent onsite follow-up, mentorship, supportive supervision, and the use of standardized tools for patient monitoring and reporting have significantly improved data quality and utilization in many settings. Close follow-up and intensive supportive supervision are necessary for the long-term sustainability of data quality improvement (DQI) efforts. Establishing DQI teams within health facilities and engaging stakeholders at all levels, such as through communities of practice or technical working groups, can enhance accountability, secure stakeholder buy-in, and facilitate the sharing of best practices. This approach strengthens the implementation of data use and DQI activities. DQI activities should be integrated into existing service delivery and quality management structures. Leveraging continuous quality improvement (CQI) processes to support DQI ensures continuity of activities and minimizes the need for additional resources. CQI relies on performance measurement and analysis to improve service delivery, which depends on accurate, valid, and complete data. In the context of HIV patient monitoring, quality improvement efforts aim to achieve better health outcomes, including effective linkage to ART initiation after diagnosis, retention on ART, and VL suppression. These outcomes rely on accurate, timely, and complete data for measurement and appropriate clinical follow-up. Countries should establish data quality assurance (DQA) and assurance processes for key HIV indicators and individual-level patient monitoring data to ensure consistency, accuracy, completeness, and timeliness. Routine DQAs should align with national reporting requirements. Strengthening data quality and utilization across the entire cascade of HIV services is essential for ensuring the quality and continuity of HIV care. DQA activities should target programmatic priority indicators, integrating HIV testing, treatment, and VL testing data to improve service quality and treatment outcomes. In 2018, WHO, UNAIDS, PEPFAR, and The Global Fund developed a joint DQA tool to harmonize and consolidate approaches for reviewing, assessing, and validating reported data on people living with HIV receiving ART (the second “95” of the 95–95–95 targets). These reviews focused on national-level aggregated data and the patient monitoring systems generating these data. The process ensured that the health ministry led the overall review and remedial actions, with defined roles for all stakeholders. A second module, published in 2020, enabled routine assessment of VL measurement data (the third “95” of the 95–95–95 targets) combined with service delivery and quality assessments of VL monitoring. Both tools include data completeness and consistency checks, as well as verification of ART and VL suppression indicators, with supportive actions to strengthen HIV patient monitoring systems. Enhanced data analysis and utilization can provide additional insights to address quality-of-care issues, better understand service delivery gaps, improve program management and surveillance, and inform policy decisions. Data use at the point of collection improves clinical care and management, strengthens health services, and enhances data quality. Examples of data use include patient management reports, facility management reports, nationally required reports, and staff accountability reports. Data can also inform service delivery quality, district outcomes, epidemiological trends, and policy changes. To promote data use in health facilities, opportunities should be created to review and discuss collected data. Regular meetings with consistent feedback to facility staff on data interpretation and implications for patient care and management are critical. Depending on the context and available tools, data use can be facilitated by dashboards for data visualization and by sharing performance reports and other information products. Standardized information products should be developed to communicate key messages from the data and support follow-up actions. These products should be pilot-tested to ensure they are useful and understandable for healthcare providers and facility staff involved in data entry and reporting. Training, mentorship, and supportive supervision are essential to improve data use at different levels. Data users should understand the information being collected and generated, as well as the source documents. They should possess basic skills to analyze and interpret data effectively. Supportive supervision involves regular onsite visits to health facilities. District meetings with representatives from each facility can showcase data, share successes, and address challenges.
